name: Auburn
lede: Auburn is a reddish brown used above all for hair, and it began as a word for something paler: a yellowish or brownish white.

sections.title: A word that changed color
sections.body:
The word comes from the Latin *albus*, white, and first described a yellowish or brownish white [1]. Its meaning moved in the sixteenth century, perhaps helped by a spelling in *abrun*, which looks like "brown" [1]. St Clair agrees on the shift from a pale off-white to a deeper ruddy brown across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries [2].

The modern word is used mostly of hair: a brownish red, sometimes golden brown [1]. The swatch here is a mid reddish brown, close to [[russet]] and [[chestnut]] and lighter than [[mahogany]].

sections.title: Hair, and the trouble with shades
sections.body:
Redheads are often described by a vocabulary of near-synonyms, and St Clair notes how elusive the exact shade of a famous redhead's hair is, called strawberry blonde in one portrait, red-gold in another and coppery auburn in a third [2]. Auburn is one point on that scale, not a fixed color.

One medieval note is worth knowing: Pastoureau's discussion of knights' epithets glosses a *roux* knight, translated there as auburn, as treacherous and hypocritical [3]. That is a literary stereotype of red hair, not a description of a dye.

sections.title: In painting
sections.body: Ball describes the young Turner's early *Fisherman at Sea* as dominated by light seeping through auburn and violet storm clouds [4]. The word is the author's description of the colors, so it names an impression, not a pigment. For a pigment-based neighbor look at [[sienna]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds the color in 2,200 of 23,781 paintings, about 9 percent [5]. It is most over-represented in the 1200s, where it is found in 22 of 142 paintings, about 3 times the museums' baseline [5]. The most devoted painter is George Catlin, in 9 of 50 works here [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [5].

origin.named_after: Latin albus (white); sense shifted in the 1500s
